sentences.text: Chilantaisaurus was a large theropod dinosaur that measured 11 meters in length and weighed between 2.5 and 4 metric tons.
Its known forelimb bones include a humerus that is among the largest found in any theropod dinosaur.
The animal possessed long hindlimbs with a robust metatarsus, which is the largest known among purported megaraptorans or Neovenator.
A unique feature is a crescent-shaped, pitted muscle scar on the anterior surface of the humeral deltopectoral crest.
Fossils were first discovered in 1960 at the Tashuikou site in Inner Mongolia, China, by a Sino-Soviet expedition.
The remains found at Tashuikou consisted of fragmentary forelimb and hindlimb bones cataloged as IVPP V.2884.1.
The genus Chilantaisaurus was formally described by the Chinese paleontologist Hu Show-Yung in 1964.
In that same year, Hu described the Tashuikou fossils as the new species Chilantaisaurus tashuikouensis.
The holotype specimen was discovered by a joint Sino-Soviet expedition in Inner Mongolia within the Ulansuhai Formation.
The original describer Hu classified Chilantaisaurus as a carnosaur, but this classification has been challenged by later studies.
A 2010 study by Benson, Carrano, and Brusatte classified Chilantaisaurus as a member of the clade Neovenatoridae within Megaraptora.
Several authors have proposed an earlier origin for the clade Neovenatoridae than suggested by Benson and colleagues.
In 2012, Allain and colleagues classified Chilantaisaurus within Spinosauridae based on traits such as a high humeral to femoral length ratio and an enlarged manual ungual.
The fossil range of Chilantaisaurus is the Upper Cretaceous.
Chilantaisaurus fossils date to the Late Cretaceous period, specifically younger than approximately 92 million years ago.
The Ulansuhai Formation containing these fossils is estimated to date from the Santonian to Campanian stages, between 85.7 and 72.2 million years ago.
The environment where the dinosaur lived was a floodplain characterized by meandering rivers, as indicated by the red mudstone and siltstone of the formation.
The exact age of the Ulansuhai Formation is currently debated among researchers.
Several fossils originally assigned to C. tashuikouensis by Hu are now considered indeterminate because they do not overlap with the main type material.
There is an ongoing debate regarding the classification of Chilantaisaurus, with proposals ranging from spinosaurid to coelurosaurian or carcharodontosaurian affinities.
Recent studies suggest that C. zheziangensis is likely an indeterminate therizinosaur rather than a species of Chilantaisaurus.
The species C. maortuensis has been reclassified multiple times, moving from Alashansaurus to Shaochilong, where it is classified as a carcharodontosaurid.
